Timeline::index¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

TimelineIndexAccessor Timeline::index(bool require_sorted = true) const

Treat Temporal Values As An Axis¶

index() is the public entrance to Timeline’s ordered-axis operations. A Timeline normally represents temporal values: it may be scalar, multidimensional, unordered, or contain NaT. An index has a narrower job. It must be a one-dimensional sequence of present instants, and it is nondecreasing unless the caller explicitly requests an unchecked accessor.

Open the dedicated Timeline Index Accessor API Reference for the complete ordered-axis method index and the individual teaching page for every accessor operation.

The returned object owns a cheap Timeline handle. Construct it once and retain it when several index operations belong to the same workflow:

const auto index = timestamps.index();

const auto insertion = index.searchsorted(key);
const auto previous = index.asof(key);
const auto bins = index.resample_bins("D");

The monotonic scan occurs at accessor construction. The later calls reuse that validated state. Ordered lookup, as-of matching, alignment, rolling windows, and resampling describe how temporal values are being used; they do not create another temporal dtype.

Parameter¶

Parameter

Meaning

Default

require_sorted

Validate nondecreasing epoch order while building the accessor

true

Passing false skips only the ordering test. Rank-one and present-value requirements remain mandatory. It neither sorts nor deduplicates the receiver.

Validation Contract¶

Property

Contract

Rank

Exactly one; scalars and matrices are rejected

Length

Any nonnegative length, including zero

Values

Every lane is a defined instant; NaT is rejected

Ordering

Nondecreasing by default; adjacent duplicates are valid

Shape

The original vector shape [n] is retained

Timezone

Retained exactly

Precision

Signed 64-bit epoch nanoseconds are retained exactly

Ordering and uniqueness are independent. Duplicate timestamps satisfy the default contract because previous <= current; call is_unique() when an algorithm requires one key per instant.

Example: Reuse One Validated Accessor¶

const auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2025-01-01T09:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-01T12:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-02T09:00:00Z",
});
const auto index = times.index();
const auto key = pluss::timeline::make("2025-01-01T10:00:00Z");

std::cout << "insert=" << index.searchsorted(key)
          << " asof=" << index.asof(key)
          << " increasing=" << std::boolalpha
          << index.is_monotonic_increasing() << '\n';

Output¶

insert=1 asof=0 increasing=true

The three operations use one checked axis. Repeatedly constructing temporary accessors would repeat the validation work.

Example: Duplicates And Empty Axes¶

const auto duplicates = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-03T00:00:00Z",
}).index();
const auto empty = pluss::timeline::epoch({0}).index();

std::cout << "duplicate_size=" << duplicates.size()
          << " unique=" << std::boolalpha << duplicates.is_unique() << '\n';
std::cout << "empty_size=" << empty.size()
          << " increasing=" << empty.is_monotonic_increasing() << '\n';

Output¶

duplicate_size=3 unique=false
empty_size=0 increasing=true

An empty vector is ordered vacuously. The {0} argument supplies a rank-one shape; a scalar Timeline has shape [] and is rejected.

Example: Inspect An Unordered Axis¶

const auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2025-01-03T00:00:00Z",
    "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z",
});

try {
  (void)times.index();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "checked=rejected\n";
}

const auto unchecked = times.index(false);
std::cout << "unchecked_increasing=" << std::boolalpha
          << unchecked.is_monotonic_increasing() << '\n';

Output¶

checked=rejected
unchecked_increasing=false

The unchecked accessor preserves the original order. Binary-search operations do not become meaningful merely because validation was skipped. Prefer times.sort().index() when ordered lookup is the goal.

Example: Borrowed Storage And Timezone Survive¶

auto* ticks = static_cast<std::int64_t*>(
    std::malloc(3 * sizeof(std::int64_t)));
ticks[0] = 0;
ticks[1] = 1'000'000'000LL;
ticks[2] = 2'000'000'000LL;

const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> shape{3};
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> strides{1};
const auto times = pluss::Timeline::from_buffer(
    ticks, shape, strides, [](void* p) { std::free(p); },
    "America/Edmonton");
const auto index = times.index();

ticks[1] = 1'500'000'000LL;
std::cout << "tz=" << index.timeline().tz()
          << " middle=" << index.host()[1] << '\n';

Output¶

tz=America/Edmonton middle=1500000000

Packed borrowed storage remains shared. Callers therefore must not mutate an external buffer in a way that invalidates ordering while a checked accessor is in use. A permanent Timeline-level monotonicity cache would be unsafe until borrowed storage is immutable or version-aware.

Failure Modes¶

index() throws when the receiver is scalar, has rank greater than one, contains NaT, or violates the requested ordering contract. Passing false relaxes only the final condition. No path silently reshapes, sorts, removes duplicates, or substitutes absent instants.

Compatibility¶

TimelineIndexAccessor is currently a source-level name for the public TimeIndex compatibility object. to_timeindex() remains temporarily available as a forwarding spelling while downstream components migrate. New code should use index(); compatibility names will be removed only after the SDK no longer exposes TimeIndex as a value dtype.
